questions.stem: Your product team builds case-management software for a defence client. From next month, any work touching the live data set must be done by a security-cleared engineer. Vetting takes about ten weeks. Two of your seven engineers hold clearance, and roughly half the next quarter's backlog touches live data. Your delivery manager proposes starting vetting for everyone and continuing to pull stories in priority order until the clearances arrive. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Re-order the backlog so the next ten weeks draw on work that does not touch live data, while vetting runs for a named group.
options.rationale: A constraint with a known lead time is a sequencing problem before it is a staffing one. Ten weeks of non-restricted work is available now, so the clearances arrive as capacity rather than as a rescue.

options.text: Start vetting for all seven engineers and keep pulling stories in strict priority order.
options.rationale: This treats clearance as paperwork running quietly in the background. Priority order will pull live-data stories to two engineers immediately, and the rest of the team will queue behind them while nominally being available.

options.text: Ask the client to allow uncleared engineers to work on live data under a cleared engineer's supervision.
options.rationale: It asks a stakeholder to relax a control the project does not own, on the project's own convenience. Requesting an exemption you would refuse in their position spends credibility badly.

options.text: Bring in two already-cleared contractors from an agency for the quarter.
options.rationale: It buys through a gap rather than sequencing around it, and it leaves your own engineers uncleared for the next time the constraint appears. Reasonable as a supplement, wrong as the first move.

questions.explanation: When access to work is gated by something with a fixed lead time, the lead time is the plan. The first question is what can be done during it, not who can be hired to bypass it, because re-ordering is free and buying is not. A constraint you can see ten weeks out has already given you the only thing it will ever give you, which is notice.
questions.mindset: A known lead time is notice, and notice is meant to be spent on sequencing.

questions.stem: Your pharmaceutical stability study runs for eleven months. The central assay may only be run by an analyst holding current competency accreditation, and the laboratory has two. One analyst's accreditation expires in month four; renewal needs a four-week assessment booked with an external body, and the next open assessment slot is month seven. Protocol sampling points fall in months three, six, nine and twelve. What should the project manager do now?

options.text: Book the month seven assessment immediately and plan the month six sampling point around the one analyst who remains accredited.
options.rationale: The expiry date and the assessment slot are both known, so both belong on the schedule. Booking now protects months nine and twelve, and month six is covered by planning for single-analyst capacity rather than discovering it.

options.text: Move the month six sampling point to month seven so that both analysts are available for it.
options.rationale: It changes the scientific protocol to suit a staffing problem. The sampling schedule is the study, and shifting a point to fit resource availability makes the data answer a different question.

options.text: Ask the laboratory manager to let the lapsed analyst run the assay supervised by the accredited one.
options.rationale: It treats accreditation as an administrative formality rather than the basis on which the result is admissible. Supervised work by an unaccredited analyst puts every sample run under it at risk of being discarded.

options.text: Note the expiry on the risk register and raise an issue if the accreditation lapses before renewal.
options.rationale: A dated certainty is not a risk. Recording it and waiting spends the months in which the assessment slot could have been booked, and by the time it becomes an issue the only options left are bad ones.

questions.explanation: A resource that carries a renewal, expiry or re-certification date is a scheduled constraint, not an uncertainty, and it belongs on the schedule with the same standing as a delivery milestone. The planning move is to book the renewal against its own lead time and to plan the interval on reduced capacity. Treating a date you already know as something to monitor converts foresight into an issue log entry.
questions.mindset: Put the expiry dates of your people's qualifications on the schedule, because a date you know is not a risk.

questions.stem: Your automotive engineering programme holds twelve floating licences for the crash simulation suite, shared by twenty engineers. Solver jobs queue, and engineers have started launching jobs early and leaving them running to hold a licence. Average waiting time has risen to about ninety minutes and utilisation of the licence pool reads as ninety-eight per cent, which the finance lead cites as evidence the pool is correctly sized. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Measure how much of the recorded licence usage is jobs held idle, before deciding whether more licences are needed.
options.rationale: Ninety-eight per cent utilisation with hoarding in it measures the hoarding, not the demand. Separating held time from solving time turns a contested number into a basis for either buying licences or changing the checkout rules.

options.text: Buy eight more licences so that every engineer has one available at all times.
options.rationale: It sizes the pool to the behaviour rather than the work, and hoarding will simply expand into the new licences. Buying against a corrupted measurement usually buys the same problem at a higher cost.

options.text: Accept the finance lead's reading and schedule simulation work into two shifts to spread demand.
options.rationale: It builds a shift pattern on a number nobody has checked. Shift working is a real cost to real people, and imposing it to solve a queue that is partly artificial is a heavy answer to an unexamined question.

options.text: Instruct engineers to stop holding licences and monitor compliance through the usage logs.
options.rationale: It treats a rational response to scarcity as misconduct. People hoard because waiting ninety minutes twice a day is worse than hoarding, and the instruction will be quietly ignored while the underlying scarcity is untouched.

questions.explanation: A high utilisation figure only means the resource is busy, not that it is productive, and contention reliably produces behaviour that inflates the figure. Before sizing a shared resource, establish what the recorded usage actually contains. The general rule is that a measurement taken from a system where people are competing for the thing being measured describes the competition as much as the demand.
questions.mindset: Ask what a utilisation figure is actually counting before you let it justify spending.

questions.stem: Three teams on your telecoms billing replacement share a single end-to-end integration environment. There is no booking system; teams take it when they need it and hold it until they are finished. Two situations have arisen in the same fortnight and the programme board has asked how each will be handled. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Two teams need the environment in the same week and both have already committed to a release date that depends on it. The project manager should
One team has held the environment for nine days while waiting for a supplier to deliver test data. The project manager should

options.text: publish a booking schedule for the environment so that contention is visible before delivery dates are committed
options.rationale: The commitments were made without anyone being able to see the clash, which is the actual failure. A visible schedule moves the conflict to the point where it can still be resolved cheaply, before dates are promised.

options.text: reclaim the environment and return that team to the queue until its dependency is ready
options.rationale: Holding a shared resource while blocked on someone else converts one team's waiting into everybody's waiting. Occupancy is not use, and the queue should be ordered by readiness to work.

options.text: commission a second integration environment for the remainder of the programme
options.rationale: Not used. Duplicating the environment is the right answer to chronic structural contention across a long programme, but it solves neither situation here: one is an unmanaged booking process and the other is an idle hold.

questions.explanation: A shared physical or technical resource needs two things that are often confused: a way to see future demand before commitments are made, and a rule that occupancy ends when productive use ends. Adding capacity is a third, separate decision, and reaching for it first hides which of the two disciplines was missing. Most environment contention is a scheduling and release problem wearing the costume of a capacity shortage.
questions.mindset: Make contention for a shared resource visible before dates are promised, and treat holding without using as not using.

questions.stem: Your public sector digital team works in two-week iterations and has held a steady throughput for six months. Looking ahead, you notice that across the two iterations covering the second half of August, five of the team's nine members are on approved annual leave for at least a week each. The product owner has drafted iteration goals for that period at the team's usual size. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the team forecast those two iterations against the capacity actually available, and set the goals from that.
options.rationale: Approved leave is known capacity, not an unknown. Forecasting from the people who will be present keeps the commitment honest and lets the product owner choose what fits rather than discover what did not.

options.text: Keep the goals as drafted and ask the team to make up the shortfall on either side of the leave period.
options.rationale: It quietly converts other people's leave into overtime for those who remain. It also protects a forecast that was wrong when it was written, which teaches the team that the forecast is a target rather than a prediction.

options.text: Ask two of the five to move their leave so that the team can hold its usual size.
options.rationale: It puts the plan ahead of approved leave that people have arranged their lives around. Doing this once buys a fortnight and costs the trust that makes people tell you about constraints early.

options.text: Bring in contractors for August to keep the team at nine.
options.rationale: It confuses headcount with capacity. New people in a stable team consume the remaining members to onboard them, so August ends with fewer effective hands than simply planning smaller would have given.

questions.explanation: Capacity is the people who will actually be there, and known absence reduces it before the period begins rather than after. Planning at nominal size through a period of approved leave is not optimism, it is a forecast that has ignored information already in hand. The transferable habit is to build every forward forecast from a capacity figure that reflects the calendar, holidays and leave included.
questions.mindset: Forecast from the people who will be present, not from the size of the team on paper.

questions.stem: Your streaming platform team is split between London and Bengaluru. The London members work 09:00 to 17:00 local time. The Bengaluru members work 09:30 to 18:30 India Standard Time, which is five and a half hours ahead of London. The team has been scheduling design discussions wherever they fall and several have run with half the team absent. Work out the collaboration window that actually exists on a normal five-day week.

blanks.label: Overlapping working hours per day, in hours
blanks.rationale: Bengaluru works 09:30 to 18:30 IST, which is 04:00 to 13:00 London time. London works 09:00 to 17:00. The two windows overlap from 09:00 to 13:00 London, which is four hours.

blanks.label: Overlapping working hours per five-day week, in hours
blanks.rationale: Four hours a day across five days gives twenty hours. That figure, not the combined headcount, is the real budget for anything the two halves of the team must do together.

blanks.label: The single word describing the kind of work that should be reserved for the overlap window
blanks.rationale: Anything needing both halves present at once is synchronous work, and it is the only thing the overlap can buy. Review, documentation and independent build are asynchronous and should be pushed outside the window.

questions.explanation: On a distributed team the scarce resource is not hours worked but hours worked at the same time, and that quantity can be calculated rather than guessed. Once it is known it should be treated like any other constrained resource: measured, protected and spent only on work that genuinely requires it. Teams that never do this arithmetic spend their overlap on status reporting and then hold design discussions in whatever slot is free.
questions.mindset: On a split team, overlap is the scarce resource, so measure it and spend it only on what needs everyone at once.

questions.stem: Your project upgrades the packing lines at a Dutch food processing plant. The schedule assumes weekend working through the changeover period. Late in planning, the site's works council agreement is confirmed to cap weekend working at one Saturday in four per employee, with no Sunday working. Your schedule needs three consecutive weekends from a crew of twelve. The site director says the council would probably agree if asked in the right way. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Re-plan the changeover against the one-in-four cap, then present the schedule impact and any request for variation with the cost of both set out.
options.rationale: The agreement is the operating constraint until it is formally changed, so the honest baseline is built on it. Asking for a variation is legitimate, but only alongside the plan that does not need one, so the council is choosing rather than being pressed.

options.text: Ask the site director to obtain the council's agreement, and keep the current schedule while that is pursued.
options.rationale: It leaves the baseline resting on a permission nobody has given. If the answer is no, the schedule was wrong for however long the conversation took, and the project finds out at the point of least flexibility.

options.text: Rotate the crew so that no individual exceeds the cap, drawing extra staff from the plant's other lines.
options.rationale: It reads the cap as an individual limit to be engineered around rather than a collective agreement. Pulling operators from running lines also moves the disruption somewhere it is not being tracked.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor that the works council agreement is blocking the changeover and request a decision.
options.rationale: It frames a normal constraint as an obstruction and hands the sponsor a problem without options. Escalating before you have re-planned tells the sponsor only that you would like the constraint removed.

questions.explanation: Labour agreements, statutory limits and site rules are constraints on availability in exactly the way that machine capacity is, and a plan that assumes they will be relaxed is not a plan but a request. Build against the constraint first, cost it, and then let anyone with the standing to seek a variation see what the variation is worth. Negotiating from a re-planned position is also the only way to know what to offer.
questions.mindset: Plan against the constraint as it stands, then let the case for changing it be argued on what it costs.

questions.stem: Your medical device software programme has run at roughly fifty-five hours a week for eleven weeks to hold a submission date. Output measured in completed features has stayed flat for the last four weeks, while defects found in integration testing have roughly doubled. The engineering lead reports that two of the nine engineers have started making errors in areas they know well. The submission is six weeks away. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Return the team to normal hours and re-forecast the submission from the output rate actually being achieved.
options.rationale: Flat output with rising defects means the extra hours are no longer producing anything, so removing them costs no real capacity. Re-forecasting from measured output replaces a date held up by effort with one held up by evidence.

options.text: Quantify the rework created by the doubled defect rate and put that figure in front of the sponsor with the date decision.
options.rationale: The sponsor is currently choosing between a date and a delay without knowing that the overtime is buying negative capacity. Rework hours make the trade visible in the only terms that can change the decision.

options.text: Add three contract engineers for the final six weeks to increase capacity without extending hours.
options.rationale: Six weeks from a regulated submission, new engineers consume the people who are already making errors. It answers a quality problem with an onboarding burden and treats headcount as interchangeable with capability.

options.text: Introduce a second review stage on all code changes to catch the additional defects before integration.
options.rationale: It builds a filter for a defect stream instead of stopping the fatigue producing it, and the reviewing is done by the same tired engineers. Inspection added at the end of an exhausted process usually just moves where the misses happen.

options.text: Hold the hours for two more weeks and reassess once the current integration cycle completes.
options.rationale: It waits for more evidence when four weeks of flat output and doubled defects is already the evidence. Two more weeks at this rate spends the very capacity that would be needed to recover.

questions.explanation: Sustained overtime buys real output for a short period and then stops, and the point at which it stops is visible in output and defect data rather than in how hard people say they are working. Once the curve has turned, hours are being converted into rework, which is worse than idleness because it also consumes the correction capacity. The management task at that point is to re-forecast honestly and let the people funding the date see what the effort is actually purchasing.
questions.mindset: Watch what the extra hours are producing, because past a point they buy rework rather than progress.

questions.stem: You manage a leakage reduction project at a water utility. Your data analyst, named in the resource plan and funded from the project budget, is told by her functional manager on a Monday that she is moving to a regulatory return for the next six weeks. Your analysis phase starts in a fortnight. The functional manager says the return is non-negotiable and offers a junior analyst instead. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Establish what the regulatory return actually needs from her and for how long, then negotiate a split or a sequence with the functional manager.
options.rationale: Six weeks full-time is an opening position, not a measured requirement. Finding out what the return genuinely consumes is what turns an announcement back into a negotiation with something to trade.

options.text: Escalate immediately to the sponsor, since the analyst is named in the resource plan and funded by the project.
options.rationale: It goes over the functional manager's head on first contact, before anyone has tested whether the clash is real. Winning that way costs the working relationship you will need for every future assignment.

options.text: Accept the junior analyst and add contingency to the analysis phase to cover the difference in experience.
options.rationale: It absorbs the impact silently and calls it contingency. The organisation never learns that the reassignment cost anything, which makes the same substitution more likely next time.

options.text: Re-sequence the analysis phase to start after the six weeks and absorb the delay in float.
options.rationale: Re-planning around the loss before testing it treats one manager's stated position as fact. It also spends float on a constraint that may turn out to be two weeks rather than six.

questions.explanation: In a matrix, competing claims on a person are normal and the first move is to convert a stated conflict into a measured one, because the measurement usually reveals room that the announcement concealed. Escalation and re-planning are both available afterwards and are both more expensive than a conversation. Going straight to either signals that you take the first version of a constraint as the final one.
questions.mindset: Test the size of a resource conflict before you accept it, escalate it or plan around it.

questions.stem: In your payments startup, one engineer built and maintains the deployment pipeline. Releases go out cleanly, and he is quick and willing whenever something breaks. He has never taken more than three consecutive days of leave. Nobody else on the team of eight has changed a pipeline configuration. He has just asked about taking a month off in the autumn and seems apologetic about it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Use the months before the leave to have others make real pipeline changes while he is present to advise.
options.rationale: The gap between now and autumn is the asset, and it only converts into resilience if other people do the work rather than read about it. Doing it while he is there means mistakes are cheap.

options.text: Ask him to write full documentation of the pipeline before he goes.
options.rationale: Documentation captures what he knows he knows and misses the judgement built from every failure he has handled. It also lets the team believe the risk is closed while nobody has ever exercised the knowledge.

options.text: Arrange for him to be contactable during the month for pipeline emergencies.
options.rationale: It resolves the leave by cancelling most of it, and it guarantees the transfer never happens because there is never a moment when it must. It also punishes the person who raised the problem honestly.

options.text: Freeze pipeline changes for the month so that nothing needs his involvement.
options.rationale: A freeze holds only until something breaks, and the pipeline is exactly the thing whose failure cannot wait. It manages the calendar rather than the dependency, which is still there in November.

questions.explanation: A single point of failure in a team is discovered through a request for leave far more often than through a risk workshop, and the request is the opportunity rather than the problem. Knowledge transfers by being used, not by being written down, so the response is to move work to other people while the expert is still available to correct them. A dependency that has never been tested should be assumed not to have been transferred.
questions.mindset: Treat a request for leave as the test of whether anyone else can actually do the work.

questions.stem: Your programme replaces nine thousand street lighting columns for a county council. The resource plan assumes six columns per crew per week, a rate taken from the contractor's performance on a dense urban contract last year. After five weeks across a mixed rural and suburban patch, the measured rate is three and a half. The delivery director wants to add four crews immediately to recover the position. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Re-forecast the resource demand for the whole programme from the measured rate before agreeing any increase in crews.
options.rationale: The plan's crew numbers were derived from a rate, so a wrong rate makes every crew figure in it wrong. Recalculating first turns the shortfall into a known quantity rather than a number chosen to feel proportionate.

options.text: Establish whether the lower rate comes from the working conditions or from this contractor's crews, since the two lead to different responses.
options.rationale: If travel between dispersed columns is consuming the day, more crews reproduce the same rate at higher cost. If it is capability or method, the remedy is supervision and sequencing, not headcount.

options.text: Add the four crews now in proportion to the shortfall, and refine the plan once the position has stabilised.
options.rationale: It multiplies a rate nobody yet understands. Where the constraint is access, permits or traffic management rather than labour, the extra crews queue behind the same bottleneck and the cost rises without the rate moving.

options.text: Hold the plan and require the contractor to achieve the rate quoted in their tender.
options.rationale: It treats a borrowed estimating assumption as a contractual failure. The rate described a different kind of patch, so demanding it produces a dispute rather than columns, and probably corner-cutting as well.

options.text: Re-baseline the programme immediately on three and a half columns per crew per week.
options.rationale: Five weeks of early work includes mobilisation and learning, so this locks in the worst rate the programme will ever achieve. Re-baselining on a figure still moving replaces one wrong number with another.

questions.explanation: A resource plan is arithmetic performed on an assumed productivity rate, and the rate is usually inherited from a context that differed in ways nobody recorded. When actuals diverge, the first move is to recompute the whole demand on the observed figure rather than to patch the visible gap, and the second is to establish what the divergence is made of, because conditions, method and capability each call for a different remedy. Adding resource to a rate you cannot explain scales the problem along with the cost.
questions.mindset: Interrogate the rate a plan multiplies by, because a resourcing figure is a productivity assumption wearing a number.

questions.stem: Your education technology company has funded four additional engineers for your product team to meet a September launch. It is now March. Your talent partner reports that hiring for these skills has been taking about fourteen weeks from approval to start date, before any ramp-up. The head of product says the budget is approved so the capacity is available, and has already added the extra scope to the launch plan. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Plan the launch on today's team, and treat the new engineers as capacity that arrives with a start date and a ramp-up curve.
options.rationale: Money becomes capacity only when someone starts and becomes productive, and both of those have dates. Planning on the current team keeps the launch honest and lets any earlier arrival be genuine upside.

options.text: Keep the launch plan as it stands and escalate if the roles are not filled within eight weeks.
options.rationale: It plans on a lead time nobody has agreed to and sets an escalation trigger for missing an invented date. The recruitment market does not respond to escalation inside your organisation.

options.text: Convert the funding to contractors so the capacity can start within a fortnight.
options.rationale: It may be the right commercial move but it is presented here as a way to preserve a plan that was never sound. Contractors also ramp up, and deciding this before re-planning skips the question of what the team can actually deliver.

options.text: Ask the head of product which of the added scope items matter most, and sequence those first.
options.rationale: Sequencing is sensible but it accepts that all the added scope belongs in the launch. The prior question is whether the capacity it was justified by will exist at all before September.

questions.explanation: Approved budget is not capacity; it is permission to begin acquiring capacity, and the acquisition has its own lead time and its own ramp. Plans built the moment funding lands routinely count people who have not been offered a job yet. The discipline is to convert every funded role into a start date and a productivity curve before it is allowed to appear in a forecast.
questions.mindset: Funding is not capacity until someone has started and become productive, and both have dates.

questions.stem: Your rail signalling upgrade was awarded to a supplier partly on the strength of a named principal engineer whose experience with the interlocking type was set out in their bid. Six weeks into mobilisation, the supplier informs you that he has been moved to another contract and proposes a replacement with three years' relevant experience rather than eighteen. The supplier notes that the contract does not name individuals. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Assess the replacement against the capability the bid was evaluated on, and set out to the supplier what would have to change to close any gap.
options.rationale: The evaluation rested on a stated capability, so the question is whether that capability is still present and what closes the difference if not. It keeps the conversation on delivery rather than on whose contract wording was cleverer.

options.text: Insist that the named engineer is reinstated, since his experience was part of the basis of award.
options.rationale: It demands something the contract does not entitle you to and that the supplier has already allocated elsewhere. Opening on a position you cannot enforce usually ends with accepting the replacement anyway, from a weaker footing.

options.text: Accept the replacement and add a contingency allowance to the interlocking commissioning stage.
options.rationale: It prices the gap instead of managing it and leaves the supplier no obligation to close it. Contingency spent on a capability shortfall buys nothing except a slower discovery of the same problem.

options.text: Raise a formal notice of dissatisfaction and place the mobilisation payment on hold pending resolution.
options.rationale: It escalates to a commercial instrument in week six over a substitution that may be entirely workable. Contractual pressure applied before assessment tends to produce a defensive supplier and no better engineer.

questions.explanation: Key personnel move, and unless the contract binds them the remedy is not to demand the individual but to hold the supplier to the capability their bid represented. That means assessing the substitute against a stated standard and agreeing what mitigation closes any shortfall, such as mentoring, shadowing or a design review by the original engineer. Managing to capability rather than to a name is also what makes the position defensible if it does escalate.
questions.mindset: Hold a supplier to the capability you evaluated, not to the name that carried it.

questions.stem: Your insurance claims modernisation uses a delivery centre in Pune with forty engineers. Attrition there has run at about thirty per cent a year for three years, and the plan assumes replacements arrive within a month, which they do. Delivery is nonetheless slipping, and analysis shows that most rework concentrates in components that have changed hands twice or more. The centre lead points out that headcount has never fallen below thirty-eight. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Re-plan on effective capacity that accounts for ramp-up and lost context, and concentrate stable ownership on the components with the most rework.
options.rationale: Headcount held while output fell means the plan is measuring the wrong thing. Planning on effective capacity and protecting continuity where turnover hurts most attacks the mechanism rather than the number.

options.text: Work with the centre lead on retention measures and hold the current plan while they take effect.
options.rationale: Retention is worth pursuing but it acts slowly and may not act at all in that labour market. Holding the plan meanwhile means the delivery date depends on a cultural change with no date attached.

options.text: Increase headcount at the centre to forty-six to absorb the productivity loss from turnover.
options.rationale: It adds more people to a system whose problem is that people keep being new. More hands at the same attrition rate produces more handovers, and the rework concentration gets worse rather than better.

options.text: Require stronger documentation standards so that departing engineers leave a fuller record of their components.
options.rationale: It answers lost context with written artefacts, which capture decisions but not the reasoning that makes the next change safe. It also adds load to the engineers who are already stretched by covering for leavers.

questions.explanation: Headcount is a count of bodies and says nothing about how much of the team is still learning, so a stable establishment can conceal a steady loss of effective capacity. Where turnover is structural rather than temporary, the response is to plan on the capacity that actually exists and to spend continuity where the cost of losing it is highest, rather than to spread the churn evenly across everything. A resource plan that assumes people are interchangeable will always be surprised by the second handover.
questions.mindset: Count effective capacity rather than heads, because a team that is always fully staffed can still always be new.

questions.stem: Your team builds a genomics data platform and has been told it cannot have more people this year. Three separate constraints are limiting throughput, and each one is scarce in a different way. The team has capacity to address all three but wants to choose the right response to each rather than apply the same fix everywhere. Match each constraint to the response that fits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The only tester is a shared-service specialist available two days a week, so testing piles up into a batch at the end of every iteration.
Every story requires the same manual reference-data refresh, half a day each time, performed by whoever happens to be free.
The team builds quickly but cannot judge whether a result is clinically meaningful without an external adviser who answers about once a week.

options.text: Have developers work alongside the tester until they can test their own stories to the same standard
options.rationale: The scarcity is a skill held by one part-time person, and skills can be spread. Moving the capability into the team removes the queue permanently rather than negotiating for more of her days.

options.text: Spend team capacity automating the refresh so that nobody performs it
options.rationale: Repetitive, identical work that consumes a person every time is the clearest case for automation. Removing the demand is better than deciding who is least busy each time it arises.

options.text: Negotiate to bring the adviser into the team part-time so questions are answered in hours rather than weeks
options.rationale: Clinical judgement cannot be cross-skilled quickly or automated at all, so the lever is latency. Shortening the feedback loop is the only one of the three responses that applies to a capability you must keep borrowing.

options.text: Recruit an additional engineer into the team
options.rationale: Not used. It is ruled out by the headcount position, but more importantly it adds general capacity to three problems that are each about a specific scarce capability rather than a shortage of hands.

questions.explanation: When throughput is limited, the useful question is what kind of scarcity is causing it, because the responses do not substitute for one another. A transferable skill is answered by spreading it, repetitive consumption of people is answered by removing the work, and irreplaceable external judgement is answered by shortening the wait for it. Adding people is the response to a shortage of hands, which is the one situation none of these is.
questions.mindset: Diagnose what kind of scarcity you have before choosing a fix, because skill, toil and access do not respond to the same remedy.

questions.stem: Every technical design in your government digital service must be approved by the principal architect before build starts. She is thorough and rarely wrong, but the queue now runs at about three weeks and four teams are idle waiting. Her calendar is genuinely full. Your delivery director suggests asking her to prioritise your team's designs, since your service has the nearest public commitment. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Propose changing the gate itself, so that routine designs meeting published standards proceed without individual approval.
options.rationale: A three-week queue behind one person is a design of the approval process, not a shortage of her hours. Converting judgement into published standards is the only move that removes the queue for all four teams.

options.text: Ask her to prioritise your team's designs given the nearest public commitment.
options.rationale: It moves your team up a queue without shortening it, so three other teams wait longer. Competing for position in a bottleneck is how bottlenecks are made permanent, because the loudest project always has a reason.

options.text: Ask for a second architect to be recruited into the approval role.
options.rationale: It doubles the capacity of a gate whose value nobody has questioned, at real cost and a long lead time. It also assumes every design genuinely needs an architect's individual judgement.

options.text: Have teams start building while their designs are in the queue, and rework anything the review changes.
options.rationale: It converts waiting into rework and quietly makes the review advisory. If that is the right answer then the gate should be removed openly rather than bypassed by teams acting first.

questions.explanation: When a single person becomes a mandatory gate, the queue is a property of the process rather than of their diligence, and asking them to work faster or to favour one project only redistributes the wait. The durable responses are to reduce what must pass through the gate, to convert repeated judgements into standards others can apply, or to remove the gate where it is not earning its cost. Prioritising within a bottleneck feels like management and changes nothing.
questions.mindset: When one person is a mandatory gate, change what has to pass through it rather than the order of the queue.

questions.stem: Your museum refurbishment has passed its resource analysis and three separate demand conflicts have come out of it. Each one has a different amount of room in it, and the finish date matters differently in each case, so the same technique will not serve for all three. The programme board wants to see which response you propose for each. Match each conflict to the technique that fits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Two activities, both with several weeks of float, each need the same conservation technician in week twelve. The completion date must not move.
A single lifting gantry is required by three activities at once. No re-sequencing within the available float resolves it, and the completion date will have to move.
The gallery fit-out is on the critical path, the opening date is fixed by a funding condition, and the only remaining option is two crews on overlapping shifts at additional cost.

options.text: Resource smoothing
options.rationale: Float is exactly what smoothing spends. Moving activities within their float relieves the peak while leaving the critical path and the completion date untouched, which is the condition stated here.

options.text: Resource levelling
options.rationale: When demand cannot be met and float has run out, the schedule yields to the resource limit. Levelling accepts a later finish as the price of a demand profile that can actually be staffed.

options.text: Crashing
options.rationale: A fixed date on a critical path activity leaves only the option of buying duration with money. Crashing is the deliberate purchase of a shorter duration, and it is the right name for what is being proposed.

options.text: Fast tracking
options.rationale: Not used. Fast tracking overlaps activities that were planned in sequence, which is a change to the logic and to the risk carried, not a response to two activities competing for the same resource.

questions.explanation: Resource conflicts are resolved by different techniques according to two questions, and the questions come before the vocabulary: whether float remains, and whether the completion date is allowed to move. Float with a fixed date means the conflict can be absorbed inside the schedule as it stands. No float with a movable date means the schedule yields to the resource limit. No float with a fixed date leaves only the option of buying duration with money. Answering both questions first is what stops a team paying for a problem that an hour of re-sequencing would have solved.
questions.mindset: Ask what float is left and whether the date can move, because those two answers pick the technique for you.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the resource-constrained chain for your satellite payload assembly. Tasks A to D form the critical chain, and tasks E and F form a feeding chain that joins it at task C. The same test technician is required on both chains, which is what made this the constraining sequence. A project buffer already sits at the end. Select the position at which a feeding buffer should be placed.

graphic.title: A critical chain of four tasks with a two-task feeding chain joining at the third task
graphic.caption: Select a position. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between positions, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Between the end of the feeding chain and the point where it joins the critical chain
regions.rationale: A feeding buffer protects the critical chain from variation on the path that feeds it, so it belongs at the junction. Placed here, a late feeding chain consumes buffer instead of delaying task C.

regions.label: After the final task of the critical chain
regions.rationale: That is the project buffer, which the stem says already exists. Adding protection at the end does nothing for a delay entering at task C, because by then the disruption has already been absorbed into the chain.

regions.label: Between each pair of tasks along the critical chain
regions.rationale: Distributing safety between individual tasks is the practice critical chain exists to replace. Task-level padding is consumed by whichever task is running, so it never accumulates where it is needed.

regions.label: Before the first task of the feeding chain
regions.rationale: Buffer at the start delays when the feeding chain begins rather than protecting what it feeds. It postpones the work without giving the junction any absorption at all.

questions.explanation: In a resource-constrained schedule, protection is aggregated rather than spread along the path, and each buffer sits where a particular kind of variation would otherwise be transmitted onward. One buffer defends the delivery date from the constraining sequence; another defends that sequence from every path feeding into it. The general rule is that protection belongs at the boundary it defends, which is why safety distributed between individual tasks is consumed locally and never accumulates where the schedule actually needs it.
questions.mindset: Put protection at the boundary it defends, not scattered along the path it is meant to protect.

questions.stem: Your motorway resurfacing scheme has a standing establishment of eight paving crews. The resource histogram for the six weeks of the main works shows crew demand of four in week one, seven in week two, eleven in weeks three and four, six in week five and three in week six. Several week three and four activities carry float. Work out the shape of the overload before deciding what to do about it.

blanks.label: Peak crew demand in any single week
blanks.rationale: The highest weekly figure in the profile is eleven, in weeks three and four. The peak is what any levelling or smoothing decision has to bring down, so it is the first number to establish.

blanks.label: Total crew-weeks of demand above the establishment of eight
blanks.rationale: Weeks three and four each exceed the establishment by three crews, and no other week exceeds it. Three plus three gives six crew-weeks, which is the quantity that must be moved, hired or deferred.

blanks.label: The technique that relieves the peak by moving activities within their float without changing the completion date
blanks.rationale: Moving activities inside their available float relieves a peak without touching the critical path, which is resource smoothing. Levelling is the term for the case where the finish date is allowed to move.

questions.explanation: A histogram overload is described by two numbers that lead to different decisions: how high the peak is, which tells you whether any single-week solution exists, and how much total demand sits above the limit, which tells you the size of what must be relocated or bought. Reading only the peak leads to hiring for a spike that float would have absorbed. Quantifying the excess before choosing a technique is what makes the choice defensible.
questions.mindset: Measure both the height of a peak and the total work above the line, because they lead to different remedies.

questions.stem: Your sixty-person enterprise resource planning programme is entering its final phase. Workstreams will finish at different points over the next five months. There is no release plan; people have historically stayed until someone notices they have nothing to do, on the reasoning that they might still be needed. Two functional managers have asked when they get their staff back so they can plan their own year. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree release dates for each role against defined completion criteria, and publish them to the functional managers.
options.rationale: Tying release to a criterion rather than a hunch makes the date defensible and lets the receiving managers plan. It also forces the programme to say what finished actually means for each workstream.

options.text: Hold all resources until the programme closes, since late problems usually need the people who built the system.
options.rationale: It insures against uncertainty using other people's budget and other departments' plans. Retaining sixty people for a risk nobody has sized is an expensive way to avoid making a decision.

options.text: Release people as each workstream finishes, deciding at the time who is genuinely no longer needed.
options.rationale: Deciding at the moment gives the receiving managers no notice and makes each release a negotiation. It also tends to retain whoever is most visible rather than whoever is still required.

options.text: Ask the functional managers to submit their requirements so releases can be prioritised against their needs.
options.rationale: It hands the sequencing to people outside the programme, who will reasonably ask for their best staff first. Release order should follow what the programme still needs, informed but not set by the receivers.

questions.explanation: Releasing resources is a planned activity with criteria, dates and communication, in the same way that acquiring them is, and a programme that plans only the acquisition leaves the organisation absorbing the cost of its uncertainty. Publishing dates tied to completion criteria gives receiving managers something to plan against and gives the programme a reason to define completion. Holding people because they might be needed is a risk response that has never been costed against the alternative.
questions.mindset: Plan how people leave a project with the same care used to plan how they arrive.

questions.stem: Your nuclear decommissioning programme is closing out three roles over the next two months, and the right answer differs for each because the skill markets differ. Your resourcing lead wants a single rule applied to all three; you think the decision depends on how replaceable each skill is and when it will next be needed. Match each situation to the decision that fits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A radiological survey specialist finishes in three weeks and is not needed again for about ten months. The skill is scarce nationally and day rates are rising.
A commissioning engineer's task ends next month, and a sister project on the same site needs exactly that skill from the following week.
A document controller's role ends at handover. The skill is widely available and can be brought back at a fortnight's notice.

options.text: Fund a retainer or bridging assignment to keep access to the individual
options.rationale: A scarce, rising-cost skill needed again within the year is worth paying to keep access to. The comparison is not against zero but against the cost and delay of re-acquiring it in a tight market.

options.text: Redeploy directly to the sister project with a planned handover date
options.rationale: Continuous work exists for the skill on the same site, so releasing to the wider organisation loses nothing and gains an immediately productive assignment. The handover date is what stops the transfer becoming a gap.

options.text: Release at the end of the role and re-acquire from the market when needed
options.rationale: Where a skill is plentiful and the re-acquisition lead time is short, holding it is pure cost. This is the case the resourcing lead is imagining, and it is only one of the three.

options.text: Extend all three assignments to programme closure to avoid re-mobilisation
options.rationale: Not used. It applies the most expensive answer to every case regardless of scarcity, which is exactly the single rule the resourcing lead wants and the reason a single rule fails here.

questions.explanation: The decision to hold, move or release a person turns on how hard the skill is to reacquire and how soon it will be wanted again, not on a uniform policy. Scarcity plus a near-term need argues for paying to keep access; continuous demand elsewhere argues for redeployment; abundance and short lead times argue for release. Applying one rule across a mixed portfolio of skills systematically overpays for the common ones and loses the rare ones.
questions.mindset: Decide whether to hold or release a skill on how hard it is to get back, not on a standard policy.

questions.stem: Your charity is replacing its supporter database. You asked the shared technology pool for one senior integration developer for twelve weeks. The pool manager cannot release a senior but offers two junior developers for the same period at a similar total cost, saying you are getting more capacity than you asked for. Your team has one experienced developer who would inevitably supervise them. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Set out what the integration work specifically requires, and assess whether two juniors plus supervision can meet it before accepting.
options.rationale: The request was for a capability, and the offer is of hours. Testing the substitution against the actual work is the only way to know whether it helps, and it makes any refusal a stated reason rather than a preference.

options.text: Accept the two juniors, since more total capacity gives the team more room than a single senior would.
options.rationale: It treats developer hours as interchangeable regardless of the work. Integration work with unfamiliar interfaces is where inexperience costs most, and the supervision load falls on your one experienced developer.

options.text: Decline the offer and wait for a senior developer to become available in the pool.
options.rationale: It rejects the substitution without testing it and leaves the project with nothing while waiting for an availability nobody has promised. Holding out for the original request is not a plan.

options.text: Accept one junior and ask for the second slot to be converted into part-time senior time.
options.rationale: A sensible-sounding compromise proposed before anyone has established what the work needs. It negotiates over the shape of the offer rather than over whether either shape does the job.

questions.explanation: Substituting people is a question about capability against specific work, not about totals of time, and the hidden cost of a substitution usually lands on whoever is already the most capable person present. The move is to describe what the work demands, then judge the offer against that description, which also converts a resourcing disagreement into a discussion both parties can reason about. Accepting or refusing on the arithmetic of headcount skips the only question that matters.
questions.mindset: Judge a resource substitution against what the work needs, not against the hours it adds.

questions.stem: Your team of eight builds the patient portal for a chain of physiotherapy clinics: six are back-end engineers and two work on the interface. The roadmap agreed for next quarter is dominated by interface work, roughly three quarters of it. Your head of engineering says capacity is not a concern because the team's velocity has been stable for nine months and headcount is unchanged. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Profile the next quarter's backlog by the skill each item needs and set it against the team's actual composition.
options.rationale: It states demand and supply in the same units, which is the only way the mismatch becomes arguable. A total that balances can still be unworkable once the shape of the work is taken into account.

options.text: Re-sequence the roadmap so interface-heavy work is spread across the quarter while the team builds capability into the gaps.
options.rationale: Spreading the concentration buys the time that capability takes to build, and does it without asking anyone to deliver work the team cannot yet do. The sequence is the lever available immediately.

options.text: Rely on velocity, which already reflects everything the team can do and has been stable for nine months.
options.rationale: Velocity is an average over past work whose mix resembled the team. It carries no information about a quarter shaped differently, which is exactly when it is most confidently quoted.

options.text: Borrow two interface developers from another team for the quarter.
options.rationale: It relieves the quarter and leaves the team unable to maintain what it will then own. Borrowing is defensible for a genuine peak, but this is a permanent change in the product's centre of gravity.

options.text: Ask the product owner to defer the interface work until the team's composition can be changed.
options.rationale: It subordinates what the product needs to the shape the team happens to have. Deferral is a real option, but choosing it before the mismatch is even sized makes the team's convenience the planning constraint.

questions.explanation: Capacity has a shape as well as a size, and aggregate measures such as headcount and velocity conceal the shape completely. When the composition of upcoming demand differs from the composition of the team, the totals continue to reassure while the work queues behind whichever skill is scarce. The response is to compare demand and supply in the same units and then to use the levers that exist now, sequence and capability building, rather than assuming that an average which held under one mix will hold under another.
questions.mindset: Match the shape of capacity to the shape of the demand, because a total that balances can still be impossible.

questions.stem: Your car-sharing service team of six sits together in one bay and relies heavily on overhearing each other, whiteboarding on the spot and resolving questions in seconds. A building reorganisation will split the team across two floors from next month. Facilities points out that everyone gains eight per cent more desk space and that the team has video calling. Your product owner regards this as a facilities matter rather than a delivery one. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Make the case to facilities in terms of the delivery effect, and if the split stands, agree compensating practices before the move.
options.rationale: Proximity is a resource this team's way of working depends on, so the argument belongs in delivery terms rather than square metres. Preparing compensating practice in advance means the team is not improvising after the loss.

options.text: Accept the move and rely on video calling and messaging to replace the informal conversations.
options.rationale: It assumes tools substitute for proximity without testing it. The conversations at risk are the ones nobody would think to schedule, and those are precisely the ones a call does not replace.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor to have the team exempted from the building reorganisation.
options.rationale: It seeks an exemption from an organisation-wide change before making the case to the people running it. Exemption is also the only outcome it allows for, so a workable compromise never gets discussed.

options.text: Treat it as a facilities decision as the product owner suggests, and raise it if throughput falls.
options.rationale: It waits for damage that will be slow, diffuse and hard to attribute once it appears. By the time throughput moves, the seating plan is settled and the argument is much harder to make.

questions.explanation: Workspace and proximity are project resources when the way of working depends on them, and they are usually allocated by people who are optimising something else entirely and have never been told. The response is to translate the effect into the terms of the decision being made, and to prepare deliberate compensation for whatever cannot be avoided. Accepting an environmental change silently and hoping tools will cover it postpones the problem until it is unattributable.
questions.mindset: Count the conditions your team works in as resources, and argue for them in delivery terms before they are taken.

questions.stem: Your team builds and runs a human resources software product, so live incidents land on the same people who are building new features. Forecasts have been unreliable and the team is losing confidence in its own numbers. Two distinct situations have come up and the team wants a consistent way of handling each rather than reacting differently every time. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Support work consumes an unpredictable share of every iteration and the team has now missed its forecast four times running. The team should
A single major outage consumed three days of the whole team in one iteration, which is far outside the usual pattern. At the iteration review the team should

options.text: set aside a measured support allowance in every iteration, sized from what support has actually consumed over recent iterations
options.rationale: Recurring interruption is not variation, it is demand, and demand that happens every iteration should be planned rather than absorbed. Sizing it from history rather than from opinion keeps the allowance honest.

options.text: report the shortfall with the outage time shown separately, and leave the standing allowance unchanged
options.rationale: A genuine outlier should be visible as an outlier. Folding it into the standing allowance would permanently reduce forecast capacity on the strength of one event that is unlikely to repeat.

options.text: increase every story estimate so that interruptions are absorbed inside the estimates
options.rationale: Not used. Hiding support demand inside estimates makes the size of a story depend on how busy support was, which destroys the meaning of the estimates and conceals how much capacity support is actually taking.

questions.explanation: Recurring demand and exceptional events are handled differently: the first is planned into capacity from measured history, the second is reported as the exception it was so that the baseline is not quietly moved. Both are undermined by burying the interruption inside estimates, which removes the ability to see how much of the team's time is going where. Keeping interruption visible is what lets anyone decide whether the split is acceptable.
questions.mindset: Plan for the interruption that recurs and report the one that does not, but never hide either inside an estimate.

questions.stem: Your aerospace programme needs composite lay-up tooling with a twenty-two week manufacturing lead time. The design freeze is nine weeks away and the tooling is needed in week thirty. The chief engineer expects two interface dimensions to change at freeze but says the rest of the geometry is settled. Your manufacturing lead wants to place the order now to protect the date. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Order the parts of the tooling that are unaffected by the two interface dimensions, and hold those elements until freeze.
options.rationale: The lead time and the design uncertainty are both real, and they apply to different parts of the tooling. Splitting the order protects the date where the design is settled and avoids buying the parts most likely to change.

options.text: Place the full order now, accepting that two dimensions may need modification later.
options.rationale: It buys the date by committing to geometry the chief engineer has already said will move. Modifying finished tooling is usually slower and dearer than making the affected elements once, correctly.

options.text: Wait for the design freeze in nine weeks and then place a single clean order.
options.rationale: Nine weeks plus twenty-two exceeds the week thirty requirement, so this chooses a certain miss over a manageable risk. Waiting for full certainty is only free when the lead time leaves room for it.

options.text: Ask the chief engineer to freeze the two interface dimensions early so the order can be placed in full.
options.rationale: It pushes an engineering decision to suit a procurement date, which is how interfaces get frozen wrong. The dimensions are open because the knowledge is not there yet, not because nobody has decided.

questions.explanation: Where a lead time is longer than the time remaining to certainty, the choice is not between committing and waiting but about which parts of the commitment can be made now. Decomposing a long-lead item by design stability lets the settled majority proceed while the volatile minority waits, and it is available far more often than teams assume. Treating the order as a single indivisible decision is what forces the false choice.
questions.mindset: When the lead time outruns the certainty, ask which part of the commitment can be made now rather than whether to commit.

questions.stem: Your offshore wind blade repair campaign uses a structural adhesive with a six-month shelf life from manufacture, stored refrigerated. Your procurement lead has negotiated a twelve per cent saving by buying the full campaign quantity in one delivery. The campaign runs for eight months and is weather-dependent, so the schedule may extend. The saving has already been reported to the sponsor as a cost improvement. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Re-price the option as staged deliveries matched to the shelf life, and put both figures to the sponsor with the write-off risk shown.
options.rationale: The saving was calculated as though the material were durable. Showing the alternative alongside the exposure lets the sponsor decide with the perishability in view rather than discover it as a write-off.

options.text: Accept the bulk purchase and plan the campaign so that all adhesive is consumed within six months.
options.rationale: It makes a weather-dependent campaign hold a fixed date to protect a consumable. The schedule driver and the material driver have been reversed, and the weather does not negotiate.

options.text: Accept the bulk purchase and increase refrigerated storage capacity to preserve the material longer.
options.rationale: Correct storage maintains the stated shelf life, it does not extend it. Spending on storage to solve an expiry problem misreads what the six months is measuring.

options.text: Ask the supplier for a written extension of the shelf life for this batch.
options.rationale: It seeks a paper solution to a material property that governs the bond strength of a structural repair. Even if given, it transfers a technical question into a commercial assurance.

questions.explanation: A consumable with a shelf life is not a stock of value but a stock with an expiry date attached, and a purchase saving calculated without that date is not a saving. The planning move is to match delivery to consumption within the material's life and to present the true comparison, including the write-off exposure, to whoever approved the saving. The same logic applies to any resource whose value decays while it waits: licences, certifications and booked slots all behave this way.
questions.mindset: Price a perishable resource against when it will be used, not against what a full order costs today.

questions.stem: Your city-centre hotel build has a laydown area of roughly two hundred square metres and no possibility of extending it. The frame package, the facade units and the plant deliveries all peak in the same six weeks. The delivery schedule was built from each subcontractor's preferred sequence, and two subcontractors have already been turned away this month with full lorries. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Build a single delivery schedule that treats the laydown area as a shared constrained resource with booked slots.
options.rationale: Three packages optimising separately against one fixed space guarantees collisions. A single booked schedule makes the constraint visible to everyone planning against it, which is the only way slots stop being claimed twice.

options.text: Move the facade units to just-in-time delivery from an off-site consolidation point during the peak.
options.rationale: Consolidation converts a space problem into a transport and coordination cost, which is the trade available when the area genuinely cannot grow. Applying it to the bulkiest package buys the most room per pound.

options.text: Ask each subcontractor to reduce the quantity of material held on site at any one time.
options.rationale: It asks three parties to solve a shared constraint independently and gives none of them visibility of the others. Each will reduce as little as possible, because holding stock protects their own programme.

options.text: Extend site working hours so that deliveries can be spread across a longer day.
options.rationale: Longer hours may help arrivals but the constraint is standing space, not delivery windows. It also runs into city-centre restrictions and spends goodwill and money on the wrong dimension.

options.text: Add a fortnight of float either side of the peak to absorb the congestion.
options.rationale: Float absorbs uncertainty in duration, not simultaneous demand for a fixed area. The three packages still peak together and the space is still two hundred square metres.

questions.explanation: A fixed physical space is a resource with a capacity, and it needs the same treatment as a scarce person: one owner, one schedule and visible contention. Where the capacity cannot be increased, the available moves are to shift demand in time or to hold the material somewhere else, and both require a single view that no individual subcontractor can produce. Asking each party to be reasonable is not a control, because each is optimising a different programme.
questions.mindset: Treat a fixed space as a scheduled resource with one owner, because a constraint nobody schedules is one everybody double-books.

questions.stem: Lifting the final bridge segment needs a crawler crane, a specialist rigging crew and wind below a stated limit. The crane is hired at a daily rate whether it lifts or not, and the crew must be mobilised the day before. Historical data for the month gives roughly a one in three chance of any given day being outside the wind limit. Your plan has the crane on site for a single nominated day. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Book a window of consecutive days rather than one day, and price the standby cost against the cost of demobilising and returning.
options.rationale: With a one in three chance of losing any nominated day, a single-day booking is a coin toss with remobilisation as the penalty. A priced window converts an uncontrolled risk into a known and decidable cost.

options.text: Keep the single day and hold a contingency budget to cover remobilisation if the lift is lost.
options.rationale: It funds the failure rather than reducing it, and remobilising a crawler crane and a specialist crew is rarely just a cost. Availability of both on a second date is the part money does not guarantee.

options.text: Move the lift to a month with a better wind record.
options.rationale: It optimises one activity against the weather while ignoring what the lift is holding up. A bridge segment sits on the critical path of everything after it, and the delay usually dwarfs the standby saving.

options.text: Ask the crane supplier to guarantee availability on a second date at no additional charge.
options.rationale: It asks a supplier to carry a weather risk they cannot influence and did not price. Either they refuse or they price it into the rate, which is the standby cost arriving under a different name.

questions.explanation: Where a resource is expensive, mobilised in advance and usable only under conditions outside anyone's control, the plan should buy a window rather than a moment. The decision is then an explicit comparison between standby cost and the cost of losing the slot, which includes remobilisation, re-availability and the delay to everything downstream. Nominating a single day for a weather-dependent operation is a plan that only works when nothing goes wrong.
questions.mindset: For a resource that only works under conditions you do not control, buy a window and price the standby.

questions.stem: Your transport ticketing app must work on a long tail of handsets. The team owns eleven test devices, and support tickets show failures on models nobody has. The engineering manager proposes buying forty devices to cover the field distribution. Your analytics show that four handset families account for eighty-six per cent of journeys, and that most reported failures sit inside those four. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Cover the four families thoroughly with owned devices, and use a paid device cloud for the remaining tail.
options.rationale: Owning what is used constantly and renting what is used occasionally matches the spending to the usage pattern. It also keeps coverage current as the tail changes, which a one-off purchase of forty devices does not.

options.text: Buy the forty devices so that the team can reproduce any reported failure directly.
options.rationale: It buys a fixed answer to a moving distribution, and most of the devices will sit idle while the tail moves on. Ownership feels like coverage but it is only coverage of the day it was bought.

options.text: Keep the eleven devices and triage failures on unsupported handsets as they are reported.
options.rationale: It leaves the team unable to reproduce failures that are already happening, so every such ticket becomes guesswork. Reacting to reports is not a testing strategy when reproduction is the missing capability.

options.text: Publish a supported device list covering the four families and decline issues outside it.
options.rationale: It solves the resourcing question by narrowing the product's promise, which is a decision for the product owner and the business rather than a response to a device shortage.

questions.explanation: Physical test resources should be provisioned against how the product is actually used, and usage data usually shows a concentrated head and a long, shifting tail. That shape argues for owning the head, where access is constant and immediate, and renting the tail, where access is occasional and the membership changes. Buying to cover an entire distribution treats a snapshot as permanent and spends most of the money on the part that moves.
questions.mindset: Own the resources you use constantly and rent the ones you use occasionally, and let usage data draw the line.

questions.stem: Your research consortium has been allocated forty thousand accelerator hours for the coming quarter, and unused hours do not carry forward. The experimental plan approved by the steering group contains one hundred and thirty training runs, each estimated at three hundred and twenty accelerator hours. The principal investigator believes the allocation is comfortable because no run has ever been refused. Work out where the plan actually stands against the allocation.

blanks.label: Total accelerator hours the approved plan requires
blanks.rationale: One hundred and thirty runs at three hundred and twenty hours each gives 41,600 hours. Nobody had multiplied it out, which is why the allocation felt comfortable.

blanks.label: Shortfall against the allocation, in accelerator hours
blanks.rationale: 41,600 required against 40,000 allocated leaves the plan 1,600 hours short. The gap is small in percentage terms and absolute in effect, because the quarter simply ends.

blanks.label: Number of complete runs that fit within the allocation
blanks.rationale: 40,000 divided by 320 gives exactly 125 runs. The five runs beyond that have no hours behind them, so the choice of which five to drop is a plan decision rather than an operational one.

questions.explanation: A consumable allocation that does not carry forward behaves like a fixed-capacity resource with a hard deadline, and the fact that no individual request has been refused says nothing about whether the total fits. The discipline is to total planned consumption against the allocation at the start of the period, because the decision about what to cut is far better made deliberately in week one than discovered in the final fortnight. Aggregate demand is invisible to anyone approving requests one at a time.
questions.mindset: Total the demand against a fixed allocation before the period starts, because nobody refusing individual requests means nothing about the sum.

questions.stem: Commissioning your water treatment plant upgrade starts in eleven weeks. Commissioning teams routinely consume instruments, seals and control cards during setting to work. Your procurement lead states that spares are an operations budget item under the asset handover policy and will be purchased by the operator after handover. The operations manager agrees, and adds that his budget year begins two months after commissioning starts. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Identify the items commissioning itself will consume and secure them as project resources, keeping the operational spares holding separate.
options.rationale: Two different things share the word spares: material consumed to complete the project work, and stock held for the asset in service. Separating them resolves the policy question without needing anyone to change a budget.

options.text: Ask the operations manager to bring forward his spares purchase so the items are on site for commissioning.
options.rationale: It asks another department to fund project consumption from a budget year that has not started. Even a willing manager cannot spend money that does not yet exist, so the request costs eleven weeks.

options.text: Escalate the handover policy to the sponsor as a blocker to commissioning.
options.rationale: The policy is not wrong, it is being applied to something it does not cover. Escalating a policy dispute is slower and more damaging than distinguishing the two categories of material.

options.text: Start commissioning as planned and raise a variation when the first consumable is needed.
options.rationale: It walks into a stoppage that is entirely foreseeable, with a commissioning team on site. Discovering the gap mid-activity converts an eleven-week procurement question into a standing-time claim.

questions.explanation: Materials consumed in order to complete project work are project resources, whoever will own the asset afterwards, and confusing them with the operational stock held for the asset in service is a recurring source of stoppages at handover. Resolving it means naming the two categories rather than arguing about who pays, because the policy usually turns out not to conflict at all. Anything the project will consume before handover has to be in the project's own resource plan.
questions.mindset: Whatever the project consumes to finish its own work is a project resource, no matter who owns the asset at the end.

questions.stem: Your fibre rollout depends on a subcontractor's splicing crews. Comparing their published programme with two other clients' schedules, you calculate that their committed crew-weeks exceed their total crew establishment by around fifteen per cent across the next quarter. You are their smallest client. Your delivery lead wants to escalate to their managing director and secure a written commitment to your dates. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Verify the capacity calculation with the subcontractor, then reduce your own exposure through re-sequencing and a second supplier for part of the work.
options.rationale: An over-commitment across three clients cannot be resolved by whichever client asks most firmly. Confirming the arithmetic and then changing your own dependency is the only lever you actually hold as the smallest customer.

options.text: Escalate to the managing director and obtain a written commitment to your dates.
options.rationale: A written commitment does not create crews. It converts a capacity shortage into a contractual position you can argue about later, while the work still does not get spliced this quarter.

options.text: Offer a rate premium in exchange for priority allocation of crews.
options.rationale: It bids for position in a queue that is over-subscribed, against larger clients who can bid more. It also rewards the over-commitment and tells the supplier that scarcity is profitable.

options.text: Raise the shortfall on the risk register and monitor the subcontractor's weekly progress against your programme.
options.rationale: Monitoring reports the failure earlier without changing it, and this is a calculated certainty rather than a risk. Watching a resource shortfall arrive is not a response to it.

questions.explanation: When a supplier has committed more capacity than it holds, the shortfall will be allocated by their commercial priorities rather than by your escalation, and a small client's leverage is close to nil. The available moves are all on your own side of the boundary: verify the constraint, reduce what depends on it, spread the dependency, or change when you need it. Assurance of a supplier's capacity is a planning input, not something to discover from their progress reports.
