questions.mindset: Check that a supplier holds the capacity they have promised, and when they do not, change your exposure rather than your tone.

questions.stem: Installing your semiconductor deposition tool requires two field engineers from the manufacturer's plant in Japan. Their work visas take eight to fourteen weeks, and the installation window opens in twelve weeks. It cannot slip without losing the fabrication ramp. The manufacturer says the applications are in hand and this is a routine matter for them. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Obtain the actual application submission dates and the reference numbers, and track them as a milestone on the project schedule.
options.rationale: In hand is a status, not a date. Putting the submissions on the schedule with evidence converts a supplier's reassurance into something the project can see slipping while there is still time to act.

options.text: Agree a fallback with the manufacturer now, such as additional named engineers in the application or a regional alternative.
options.rationale: The window between eight and fourteen weeks straddles the installation date, so a fallback is needed for an outcome that is more likely than not. Agreeing it now costs a conversation; agreeing it in week eleven costs the ramp.

options.text: Add four weeks of float in front of the installation window to absorb any visa delay.
options.rationale: The stem states the window cannot slip, so this invents flexibility that does not exist. Float placed against an immovable downstream commitment is float on paper only.

options.text: Engage an immigration adviser to expedite the applications on the project's behalf.
options.rationale: The applications belong to the manufacturer as the employer, and a third party cannot expedite what they have not filed. It spends money and creates a second channel that confuses the one that matters.

options.text: Rely on the manufacturer's experience, since they perform these installations worldwide and know the process.
options.rationale: Their competence is real and irrelevant to whether the grant lands before week twelve. Delegating a constraint to whoever is most familiar with it is how projects stop tracking it.

questions.explanation: Where a resource can only reach the work through a process controlled by a third party, the project's job is to make that process visible and to hold an alternative for the case where it runs long. Neither the supplier's experience nor their assurance changes the distribution of outcomes; only evidence of progress and a prepared fallback do. A stated range that straddles your need-by date should be planned as a likely miss rather than an unlikely one.
questions.mindset: When a stated lead-time range straddles your date, plan for the far end and hold an alternative.

questions.stem: A norovirus outbreak has taken six of your twenty-two staff off the contact centre migration for at least a week, and more absence is expected. The migration has a fixed cutover in three weeks driven by a lease expiry. Your plan assumed full availability throughout and holds no allowance for absence. Your workstream leads are each proposing to slow their own strand proportionally. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Identify what cutover genuinely requires, concentrate the remaining people on that, and defer everything else past the date.
options.rationale: A fixed date with reduced capacity is a prioritisation problem, and only the work that cutover depends on can keep its claim. Proportional slowing spreads the loss across essential and deferrable work alike.

options.text: Let each workstream slow proportionally, since the reduction in capacity affects all strands equally.
options.rationale: It is fair and it fails, because the date does not care about fairness between strands. Everything arrives late together, including the few things that had to be finished.

options.text: Bring in temporary staff to replace the absent people for the three weeks.
options.rationale: Three weeks before a cutover, temporary staff need briefing from the people who are still standing. It spends the scarcest capacity on onboarding at the worst possible moment.

options.text: Ask the absent staff to work from home where they are well enough to do so.
options.rationale: It presses unwell people back to work and will produce errors and a longer outbreak. It also assumes the absence is the problem to solve rather than the condition to plan within.

questions.explanation: When capacity falls against a date that cannot move, the only real lever is scope, and the decision is which work the date actually depends on. Slowing everything proportionally is the instinctive response because it avoids choosing, but it converts a partial delivery that would have met the date into a complete one that does not. Deciding what must be true at cutover, and abandoning the rest for now, is the judgement the situation demands.
questions.mindset: When capacity drops against a fixed date, choose what must be finished rather than slowing everything equally.

questions.stem: Your eight engineers on an online retail platform each lose roughly forty-five minutes a day waiting for builds and test runs on ageing laptops. A refresh would cost about £16,000 and take two weeks to arrange. Your finance business partner notes that the laptops are only three years into a four-year replacement cycle and that bringing the refresh forward needs a case. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Quantify the waiting time as capacity, compare it against the cost of the refresh, and put the case to the finance partner.
options.rationale: Six engineer-hours a day is a capacity figure the replacement cycle was never asked to consider. Turning the loss into the same units as the cost is what lets a policy exception be judged rather than merely requested.

options.text: Accept the replacement cycle and have the team use the waiting time for code review and reading.
options.rationale: It dresses up interruption as productivity. Forty-five minutes broken into many short waits does not aggregate into useful review time, and the assumption that it does is why the loss stays invisible.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor for an exception to the replacement cycle on delivery grounds.
options.rationale: It jumps to authority before making the argument to the person who owns the policy and can approve it. Escalating an unquantified claim also invites a decision based on who is more persuasive.

options.text: Move builds to cloud infrastructure so that laptop performance stops mattering.
options.rationale: It may well be the right long-term answer, but it is a larger change chosen before the size of the problem is known. Solving an unmeasured loss with an architectural project is how small costs become large ones.

questions.explanation: The tools people work with are project resources, and time lost to inadequate ones is capacity lost just as surely as an unfilled role, but it never appears in a resource plan because it is distributed in small pieces. Making the case means converting the loss into the units the decision is made in, which is usually money or people. Asset replacement policies are set without reference to what any particular team is losing, so the exception has to be argued with numbers.
questions.mindset: Add up the small losses your team's tools impose, because capacity leaking in minutes never shows up in a resource plan.

questions.stem: Your insurance team is rebuilding its quote engine. At each planning session, work is taken by whoever has finished their last item, which the team regards as a fair and simple rule. A story touching the premium calculation rules has been picked up by a developer who has never worked on them, while the two developers who know that area are on unrelated items. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Raise it with the team and suggest pairing the developer with one who knows the calculation rules.
options.rationale: It gets the work done safely and spreads the knowledge, so the same story is less risky next time. Raising it with the team rather than reassigning also keeps the decision where the working agreement lives.

options.text: Leave it, since letting people pull work freely is what keeps the team flexible and shared.
options.rationale: Pull works when the puller can do the work or can get help, and neither is arranged here. Treating a scheduling convenience as a principle means nobody has to notice when it does not fit.

options.text: Reassign the story to one of the two developers who know the premium calculation rules.
options.rationale: It gets the story done fastest and leaves the knowledge exactly where it was. Repeatedly routing work to whoever already knows it is how a team ends up with two people who can touch anything important.

options.text: Ask the developer to research the calculation rules before starting the story.
options.rationale: It substitutes solitary study for access to the people who hold the knowledge. It is slower than pairing and produces an understanding nobody has checked.

questions.explanation: Availability determines who can start work, but capability determines whether the work will go well, and a pull system needs both to be considered. Where they diverge, pairing usually resolves the tension because it delivers the item and moves the knowledge at the same time. A rule that assigns purely on who is free is easy to operate and slowly concentrates every specialism in the same few people.
questions.mindset: Who is free decides who can start, but who knows the work decides whether it should be started alone.

questions.stem: The diagram shows four activities in your school refurbishment, with each activity's float drawn as a hatched extension to its bar. The site closes completely for a two-week examination period, shown as the shaded band, and no work of any kind may take place then. The schedule was built on a calendar that treats every week as a working week. Select the activity whose float is not real once the closure is applied.

graphic.title: Four activity bars with hatched float, crossed by a shaded two-week site closure band
graphic.caption: Select an activity. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between activities, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Window replacement — two weeks of float falling entirely inside the closure band
regions.rationale: Float is only float if the days in it can be worked. Both weeks of this activity's float sit inside the closure, so the activity is in truth critical and the schedule is showing slack that cannot be used.

regions.label: Roof works — float falling in working weeks after the closure
regions.rationale: Its float lands on weeks when the site is open, so the slack is genuinely available. This is the case people generalise from when they assume all float on the chart is usable.

regions.label: Rewiring — no float shown
regions.rationale: An activity with no float cannot have float that is unreal. It is already treated as critical, so the closure changes its dates but not the way the schedule describes it.

regions.label: Decoration — float falling in working weeks before the closure
regions.rationale: Its float sits in open weeks and can be spent normally. Selecting it usually comes from reading proximity to the shaded band rather than checking where the hatched portion actually falls.

questions.explanation: Float is a statement about available working time, so it only means anything relative to the calendar the resource can actually work. Non-working periods such as shutdowns, holidays and closures must be applied to the calendar before float is read, or the schedule will show slack on activities that have none and hide criticality from everyone using it. The general check is to ask when the float falls, not merely how much of it there is.
questions.mindset: Read float against the calendar people can actually work, because slack in a week nobody works is not slack.

questions.stem: Your social housing retrofit carries a contractual commitment that at least one in ten site hours is worked by apprentices, reported quarterly to the local authority. Your delivery manager wants to suspend apprentice placements during the twelve-week insulation peak, arguing that supervision slows experienced fitters and that the ratio can be recovered afterwards. The current quarter's return is due in five weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Plan the apprentice hours into the peak with the supervision they require, and treat both as resourced elements of the programme.
options.rationale: The ratio is a delivery obligation of the contract, so the hours and the supervision they consume are part of the work rather than an overhead on it. Resourcing them explicitly is what stops them being the first thing dropped under pressure.

options.text: Suspend placements for the peak and recover the ratio in the following quarter as the delivery manager proposes.
options.rationale: It trades a reported commitment for schedule relief without anyone with the authority to make that trade being asked. The quarterly return also falls inside the peak, so the recovery comes after the report.

options.text: Seek the local authority's agreement to average the ratio across the whole contract rather than by quarter.
options.rationale: Renegotiating a reporting basis to accommodate a resourcing decision you have not yet tried to plan for spends client goodwill on the wrong thing. It also invites scrutiny of why the peak was planned without it.

options.text: Maintain the placements but assign apprentices to lower-risk work away from the insulation activities.
options.rationale: It meets the number while hollowing out the purpose, and the authority is buying skills development rather than hours logged. It is the kind of compliance that damages a relationship when it is noticed.

questions.explanation: Social value and workforce commitments written into a contract are delivery obligations with a resource cost, and that cost includes the supervision, mentoring and slower output they bring with them. Plans that treat them as a compliance overhead rather than as resourced work will always find them expendable at the first pressure point. If a commitment genuinely cannot be met, that is a conversation with the client held in advance, not a shortfall explained afterwards.
questions.mindset: Resource the commitments your contract makes about people, or they become the first thing sacrificed under pressure.

questions.stem: Your automation programme for a builders' merchant's distribution centre mobilises in eight weeks. The team of thirty has been assembled from whoever the two participating organisations could release, and every seat on the structure chart is filled. Reviewing the work ahead, you find nobody with experience of the stacker crane control protocol, and one person with partial knowledge of the warehouse control system being replaced. The steering group regards mobilisation as complete. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Assess the team against the capabilities the work actually requires and present the gaps to the steering group with their delivery consequence.
options.rationale: A full structure chart has been mistaken for a capable team, and only a comparison against the work exposes the difference. Attaching the delivery consequence is what turns a staffing observation into a decision the steering group can take.

options.text: Close the two identified gaps before mobilisation through targeted recruitment, vendor support or training with a named plan for each.
options.rationale: Eight weeks is enough for some closures and not others, and naming the route for each gap makes the timing testable. Deciding gap by gap avoids applying one remedy to capabilities that differ in how they can be acquired.

options.text: Begin mobilisation as planned and address capability gaps as they surface during the first phase.
options.rationale: It discovers a known deficiency at the point of maximum cost, with thirty people already deployed. The gaps have already surfaced; what is proposed is waiting for them to hurt.

options.text: Assign the person with partial operating system knowledge to lead that workstream and support them closely.
options.rationale: It appoints the only available candidate to the role and calls the gap closed. Support that is not specified is not a plan, and it puts one partially informed person in a position where nobody can check them.

options.text: Ask the two participating organisations to confirm that the staff they released meet the programme's requirements.
options.rationale: It asks the parties who supplied the people to mark their own work, and they will reasonably answer against their own understanding of the need. Assurance from the source of the problem is not verification.

questions.explanation: A staffed structure chart says that positions are filled, not that the capability the work requires is present, and the two are routinely confused at mobilisation because the chart is the visible artefact. The check is a comparison of the work ahead against what the assembled people can actually do, and each gap then needs its own route and lead time, since some capabilities can be trained, some must be hired and some can only be borrowed. Gaps found before mobilisation are cheap; the same gaps found afterwards are the programme's first crisis.
questions.mindset: A filled seat is not a capability, so check the team against the work before deciding mobilisation is complete.
